GMM-token PFN: propagating a known d-dim displacement GMM¶

Issue #23, branch exp/23-gmm-prop. An idea of the user's (2026-11-05), unrelated to the AIR line. Exploratory: one seed, one pilot.

Description¶

Idea. A PFN maps a d-dim input to a binned (bar) distribution over a 1-dim output. A displacement $u(x)\in\mathbb R^d$ is a d-dim output, and bins over $\mathbb R^d$ need $B^d$ cells, which is infeasible beyond d ≈ 2. Instead:

  • each context token sits at one of A's locations $x_i$ and carries a GMM over the displacement there, $q_i(u)=\sum_m w_{im}\,\mathcal N(u;\mu_{im},s_i^2 I)$ (as a probabilistic registration would give);
  • PFN self-attention between context tokens and cross-attention from queries to context propagate this knowledge;
  • the output at any query $x^*$ is a GMM over $u(x^*)$ (a mixture-density head with $K$ diagonal components: $K(2d+1)$ numbers, linear in d).

Later (not here), one samples displacements from the query's GMM, queries B's KV-cached PFN at $x^*+u$ and weights by the GMM to get a mixture over $y$. That needs a probabilistic registration, the output map h, and a weighting against the A-only predictive. This experiment tests only the propagation, with the token GMMs given.

Question. How close does a GMM-token PFN get to the exact Bayes predictive of the displacement at a new location, as a function of the dimension d and the number of context tokens n? And does the GMM head keep the joint multimodality across the d output dimensions that a per-dimension (bar-distribution) head cannot represent?

Prior (one task).

  • Dimension d (one model per d ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8}); locations $x_i, x^*\sim\mathcal U[0,1]^d$.
  • $M\in\{1,2,3\}$ displacement hypotheses with $p(M)=(0.4,0.3,0.3)$, weights $w\sim\text{Dir}(1_M)$.
  • Each hypothesis is a field $u_m:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R^d$, independent GP draws per output dimension, squared-exponential kernel, amplitude $\alpha=0.1$, length scale $\ell=\ell_0\sqrt d$ with $\ell_0\in\{0.2,0.4,0.8\}$ uniform (the $\sqrt d$ keeps typical pairwise correlations comparable across d).
  • Token i: per-token noise $s_i\sim\log\mathcal U[0.005,0.05]$; components $(w_m,\ \mu_{im}=u_m(x_i)+s_i\varepsilon,\ s_i)$, shuffled independently per token, so a token's components carry no label; correspondence across tokens has to be inferred (from smoothness and from the weights, which are shared by the hypotheses).
  • Target at a query: $m^*\sim\text{Cat}(w)$ independently per query, $u^*=u_{m^*}(x^*)$ (the noise-free displacement).
  • n ~ U{0, …, 128} per training batch; 64 queries per task.

Model. Token = MLP(embedding of $x_i$ + DeepSets sum over its components of MLP$(w,\mu/\alpha,\log(s/\alpha))$); a learned null token is always in the context (n = 0 works). Pre-LN PFN layers: every token attends to the context tokens only (queries do not see each other). Head: $K=10$ diagonal Gaussians. Inputs and outputs are in units of α. 4 layers, width 128, 4 heads. Trained by the NLL of $u^*$; AdamW, lr 3e-4, cosine with warmup, 30k steps of 64 tasks.

References on the same tasks (fixed evaluation set, CPU-generated).

  • oracle: the exact Bayes predictive given the labelled data (it knows which component of each token belongs to which hypothesis): mixture over ℓ (posterior from the GP evidence of all hypotheses) and over m (weights $w_m$) of the GP posteriors. Closed form, no MC error. With shuffled labels the true Bayes predictive also has to infer the labelling, so for M ≥ 2 this oracle is an optimistic bound (exact for M = 1).
  • oracle_fact: the product over the d output dimensions of the oracle's 1-dim marginals: the best any per-dimension head (e.g. d bar distributions) could do, bin resolution aside. Equal to the oracle for d = 1 or M = 1 with one dominant ℓ.
  • prior: $\mathcal N(0,\alpha^2 I)$, what n = 0 allows.

What to look for.

  • Metric: NLL of $u^*$ at a query (joint over the d dimensions, nats; reported also per dimension), mean over 64 queries and 256 tasks per cell; cells n ∈ {0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128}.
  • Gap Δ(d, n) = NLL_model − NLL_oracle with a 95 % bootstrap CI over tasks; Δ/d per dimension. Strata M = 1 (no correspondence problem) and M ≥ 2.
  • Joint multimodality: NLL_model − NLL_oracle_fact on M ≥ 2 tasks for d ≥ 2.
  • Sanity: at n = 0 the model must match the prior (Δ ≈ 0); the oracle's gain over the prior grows with n.
  • Qualitative: d = 1 predictive density over x with the token GMMs; d = 2 predictive density over $u^*$ at a few queries, model against oracle.

GO / NO-GO (exploratory, per d).

  • A cell (d, n) propagates if Δ/d ≤ 0.05 nats on all tasks and on the M ≥ 2 stratum.
  • GO for the GMM-token propagation if every cell with d ≤ 4 propagates and for d ∈ {2, 4} the model beats oracle_fact on M ≥ 2 tasks at every n ≥ 8 (CI excludes 0).
  • INCONCLUSIVE if this holds for d ≤ 2 only; NO-GO if d = 2 fails.
  • d = 8 is descriptive: how the gap grows.

Limits.

  • The token GMMs are given and exact in form (isotropic, shared weights across tokens); a real registration gives approximate, locally varying weights. Shared weights make correspondence easier than it will be.
  • The oracle for M ≥ 2 is optimistic (labelled), so Δ there includes the unavoidable cost of not knowing the labelling.
  • The prior is a GP on [0,1]^d; one seed; one model per d (no d-amortisation); n ≤ 128 (the training range).

Results¶

Two sweeps, the same 256 evaluation tasks per d (CPU-generated, seed 2311 + 1000 d; nested context sets, so cell n uses the first n tokens of each task), 64 queries per task:

  • registered (REG): the pre-registered setting, 30k steps, gradient clip 1.0;
  • D1 (D1): clip 20 and 60k steps, everything else unchanged (deviation D1 in the log: the clip was active at every step of the registered run, and its validation NLL was still falling). The verdict is read on the registered run.

All NLLs are per query, in nats, joint over the d displacement dimensions unless the column says "/ d".

def ci_mean(x):
    lo, hi = bootstrap_ci(np.asarray(x), n_boot=2000)
    return pd.Series({"mean": np.mean(x), "lo": lo, "hi": hi})

1. Sanity¶

How to read. Three checks that the pipeline measures what it should:

  • at n = 0 there is nothing to propagate, so model, oracle and prior must agree (Δ ≈ 0);
  • the oracle's gain over the prior must grow with n (the references are right and context is informative);
  • oracle ≤ oracle_fact everywhere, with equality at d = 1 (one dimension has nothing to factorise).

Numbers are per dimension (NLL / d), averaged over the 256 tasks.

2. NLL against the number of context tokens¶

How to read. One panel per d; x is the number of context tokens n (symlog scale, n = 0 on the left), y the NLL per dimension (lower is better). Black: the labelled oracle (optimistic for M ≥ 2); grey dashed: the best per-dimension predictor (oracle_fact); grey flat: the prior; blue / orange: the GMM-token PFN, registered and D1. The vertical gap between a coloured line and black is Δ / d; between black and grey dashed is what a factorised (bar-per-dimension) head would give up at best.

3. Gap to the oracle and the pre-registered criteria¶

How to read. Δ / d = (NLL_model − NLL_oracle) / d per cell, mean over tasks with a 95 % bootstrap CI. The criterion: a cell propagates if Δ / d ≤ 0.05 on all tasks and on the M ≥ 2 stratum. ✓ / ✗ mark it. For M ≥ 2 the oracle knows the labelling, so part of Δ there is the unavoidable cost of not knowing it (§ 5).

In [4]:
R["gap"] = R.model - R.oracle
R["strat"] = np.where(R.m == 1, "M = 1", "M ≥ 2")


def gap_table(run):
    g_all = R[R.run == run].groupby(["d", "n"]).gap.apply(ci_mean).unstack()
    g_mm = R[(R.run == run) & (R.m > 1)].groupby(["d", "n"]).gap.mean()
    out = g_all.assign(**{"M≥2": g_mm})
    out["propagates"] = np.where((out["mean"] <= 0.05) & (out["M≥2"] <= 0.05), "✓", "✗")
    return out


GT = {run: gap_table(run) for run in SWEEPS}
for run, g in GT.items():
    print(f"{run}: Δ / d (mean, CI) and M ≥ 2 stratum")
    show = g.apply(lambda r: f"{r['mean']:.3f} [{r.lo:.3f}, {r.hi:.3f}] | {r['M≥2']:.3f} {r.propagates}", axis=1)
    display(show.unstack("n"))

4. Joint multimodality: GMM head against the best per-dimension head¶

How to read. On tasks with M ≥ 2 hypotheses and d ≥ 2 the displacement at a query is a mixture of whole vectors: its dimensions are dependent (they switch hypothesis together). A per-dimension head (d bar distributions) can at best reproduce the product of the 1-dim marginals, oracle_fact. Two columns, per dimension, mean over M ≥ 2 tasks:

  • model − oracle_fact < 0 (CI excluding 0): the GMM-token PFN beats any per-dimension head; this is the pre-registered check (every n ≥ 8, d ∈ {2, 4});
  • model_fact − model ≥ 0: how much the model's own joint structure buys over its own marginals.
In [5]:
JT = {}
for run in SWEEPS:
    S = R[(R.run == run) & (R.m > 1) & (R.d > 1)].copy()
    S["vs_fact"] = S.model - S.oracle_fact
    S["own"] = S.model_fact - S.model
    a = S.groupby(["d", "n"]).vs_fact.apply(ci_mean).unstack()
    a["own"] = S.groupby(["d", "n"]).own.mean()
    a["beats"] = np.where(a.hi < 0, "✓", "✗")
    JT[run] = a
    print(f"{run}: (model - oracle_fact) / d [CI] beats? | (model_fact - model) / d")
    display(a.apply(lambda r: f"{r['mean']:.3f} [{r.lo:.3f}, {r.hi:.3f}] {r.beats} | {r.own:.3f}", axis=1).unstack("n"))

5. Where the gap sits: hypotheses and length scale¶

How to read. Δ / d by stratum for the D1 run (the better-trained model, so the pattern is less a training-budget artefact), against n. Left: number of hypotheses M (M = 1 has no correspondence problem, so its gap is pure propagation error; the extra gap at M ≥ 2 is the labelling, part of which no learner can avoid). Right: length scale ℓ₀ (short length scales need many tokens and precise interpolation).

6. Training curves¶

How to read. Validation NLL (n = 16, its own seed, joint nats) during training; registered (blue) and D1 (orange); the dashed line is the oracle on the same validation tasks. If a curve is still falling at its end, the gap in § 3 includes undertraining.

In [7]:
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, len(DS), figsize=(3.2 * len(DS), 2.6))
for ax, d in zip(axs, DS):
    vb = P.sample(256, 128, int(d), 64, torch.Generator().manual_seed(9999 + 1000 * int(d))).head(16)
    ax.axhline(-float(O.references(vb)["oracle"].mean()), color=INK, ls="--", lw=1.2, label="oracle")
    for run in SWEEPS:
        mem = ev[(ev.run == run) & (ev.d == d)].member.iloc[0]
        t = tr[(tr.run == run) & (tr.member == mem)]
        ax.plot(t.step, t.val_nll_n16, color=C[run], lw=1.5, label=run)
    ax.set_title(f"d = {d}")
    ax.set_xlabel("step")
axs[0].set_ylabel("val NLL at n = 16")
axs[-1].legend(fontsize=7)
fig.tight_layout()

7. Examples¶

The two figures are computed live on CPU from the D1 checkpoints, on tasks drawn for the figure (generator seed 7, not evaluation tasks), chosen by a fixed rule: the first draw with M = 2 hypotheses, both weights ≥ 0.3 and ℓ₀ = 0.4.

7a. d = 1: predictive density over x¶

How to read. Each column of an image is the predictive density of u(x) at that x (a dense grid of 200 queries), scaled to its own maximum (as in the PPD heatmaps of notebooks 10, 13 and 15). Dots: the context tokens' components at (x_i, μ_im), dot area ∝ weight (a token's two dots are its two hypotheses, unlabelled). Lines: the two true fields u_1, u_2 (the solid one has the larger weight). Columns: oracle (labelled) and the GMM-token PFN, for n = 4, 16 and 64. Titles: mean NLL over the 200 grid queries, with the target drawn as in training (m* ~ w).

In [8]:
CK = {d: ROOT / f"runs/gmm_prop/{SWEEPS['D1']}/{i}/tracking/artifacts/model.pt" for i, d in enumerate(DS)}


def load(d):
    m = GMMPFN(d)
    m.load_state_dict(torch.load(CK[d], map_location="cpu"))
    return m.eval()


def pick(d, n, Q, xq=None, seed=7):
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    while True:
        b, uq = P.sample_fields(1, n, d, Q, g, xq_fixed=xq)
        w = b.w_lab[0]
        if int(b.m[0]) == 2 and float(w[:2].min()) >= 0.3 and abs(float(b.ell[0]) / d**0.5 - 0.4) < 1e-4:
            return b, uq


def density_grid(p, ugrid, model):
    """[Q, G] densities of a 1-d mixture (oracle dict or model dict) on ugrid."""
    if model:
        lw, mu, sd = p["logw"][0], p["mean"][0, :, :, 0], p["logstd"][0, :, :, 0].exp()
    else:
        lw, mu, sd = p["logw"][0].float(), p["mean"][0, :, :, 0].float(), p["var"][0].float().sqrt()
    z = (ugrid[None, None] - mu[..., None]) / sd[..., None]
    lp = -0.5 * z**2 - torch.log(sd[..., None]) - 0.5 * np.log(2 * np.pi)
    return torch.logsumexp(lw[..., None] + lp, 1).exp()


M1 = load(1)
xg = torch.linspace(0, 1, 200)[:, None]
b, uq = pick(1, 64, 200, xq=xg)
ugrid = torch.linspace(-0.35, 0.35, 300)
NN = (4, 16, 64)
fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, len(NN), figsize=(3.6 * len(NN), 5.0), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for j, n in enumerate(NN):
    bn = b.head(n)
    po = O.predictive(bn)
    with torch.no_grad():
        pm = M1(bn)
    nll_o = -float(O.mixture_logpdf(po, bn.yq).mean())
    nll_m = -float(M1.log_density(pm, bn.yq).mean())
    for i, (dens, lab, nl) in enumerate([(density_grid(po, ugrid, False), "oracle", nll_o),
                                         (density_grid(pm, ugrid, True), "GMM-token PFN (D1)", nll_m)]):
        ax = axs[i, j]
        img = (dens / dens.max(1, keepdim=True).values).T.numpy()
        ax.imshow(img, origin="lower", aspect="auto", extent=(0, 1, float(ugrid[0]), float(ugrid[-1])), cmap="Blues",
                  vmin=0, vmax=1)
        order = torch.argsort(b.w_lab[0, :2], descending=True)
        for k, ls in zip(order.tolist(), ["-", "--"]):
            ax.plot(xg[:, 0], uq[0, :, k, 0], ls, color="#eb6834", lw=1.2)
        xs = bn.x[0, :, 0].repeat_interleave(P.M_MAX)
        mus, ws = bn.mu[0, :, :, 0].reshape(-1), bn.w[0].reshape(-1)
        ax.scatter(xs[ws > 0], mus[ws > 0], s=60 * ws[ws > 0], color=INK, zorder=3)
        ax.set_title(f"{lab}, n = {n}: NLL {nl:.2f}", fontsize=9)
        ax.grid(False)
    axs[1, j].set_xlabel("x")
axs[0, 0].set_ylabel("u(x)")
axs[1, 0].set_ylabel("u(x)")
print(f"weights {b.w_lab[0, :2].numpy().round(2)}, ℓ = {float(b.ell[0]):.2f}")
fig.tight_layout()

weights [0.61 0.39], ℓ = 0.40

7b. d = 2: the joint predictive of the 2-dim displacement at three queries¶

How to read. One task with M = 2 hypotheses and n = 16 tokens. Each panel is the predictive density over (u₁, u₂) at one query location (log-density contours, the darkest band holding the most mass), oracle (top) and the GMM-token PFN (bottom). Crosses: the two true displacement vectors u_1(x*), u_2(x*) (the larger cross has the larger weight). A per-dimension head would put mass on all four combinations of the marginal modes (the "ghost" modes at (u_1,1, u_2,2) and (u_2,1, u_1,2)); a joint head keeps two. Titles: log density of each true vector under the predictive.

In [9]:
M2 = load(2)
b2, uq2 = pick(2, 16, 3, seed=11)
po2 = O.predictive(b2)
with torch.no_grad():
    pm2 = M2(b2)


def at_query(p, q, G):
    # the mixture of query q, repeated for G evaluation points: every [1, Q, ...] entry becomes [1, G, ...]
    return {k: v[:, q : q + 1].expand(1, G, *v.shape[2:]) for k, v in p.items() if k != "logpost_ell"}


def logp_oracle(q, Y):
    return O.mixture_logpdf(at_query(po2, q, Y.shape[0]), Y[None])[0].float()


def logp_model(q, Y):
    with torch.no_grad():
        return M2.log_density(at_query(pm2, q, Y.shape[0]), Y[None].float())[0]


fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10.5, 6.6))
for q in range(3):
    c = uq2[0, q, :2]  # [2 hypotheses, 2 dims]
    lo, hi = c.min(0).values - 0.06, c.max(0).values + 0.06
    g1, g2 = torch.meshgrid(torch.linspace(float(lo[0]), float(hi[0]), 160),
                            torch.linspace(float(lo[1]), float(hi[1]), 160), indexing="ij")
    Y = torch.stack([g1.reshape(-1), g2.reshape(-1)], -1)
    for i, (lab, f) in enumerate([("oracle", logp_oracle), ("GMM-token PFN (D1)", logp_model)]):
        lp = f(q, Y).reshape(160, 160)
        lp_true = f(q, c)
        ax = axs[i, q]
        top = float(lp.max())
        ax.contourf(g1, g2, lp, levels=np.linspace(top - 8, top, 9), cmap="Blues")
        for k in range(2):
            ax.plot(c[k, 0], c[k, 1], "x", color="#eb6834", ms=6 + 6 * float(b2.w_lab[0, k]), mew=2)
        ax.set_title(f"{lab}, query {q}: log p = {lp_true[0]:.1f}, {lp_true[1]:.1f}", fontsize=8)
        ax.set_xlabel("u₁")
        ax.set_ylabel("u₂")
        ax.grid(False)
print(f"weights {b2.w_lab[0, :2].numpy().round(2)}, ℓ = {float(b2.ell[0]):.2f}, n = 16")
fig.tight_layout()

Verdict¶

Verdict (registered run pilot_20261105-145454, criterion as pre-registered): NO-GO. d = 2 fails: Δ / d = 0.06 at n = 2 and 0.14 at n = 4, above 0.05 from n = 2 on (§ 3); the M ≥ 2 joint check fails as well (the model is worse than the best per-dimension predictor from n ≈ 2–4 on, § 4). The longer-trained D1 run (pilot_20261105-150054) does not change the verdict, although it roughly halves the gap at d = 1, 2. Exploratory: one seed, one training budget. To be recorded by the user with just decide.

What the numbers say.

  • Sanity holds. At n = 0 model = prior = oracle (|Δ| / d ≤ 0.004); the oracle gains 0.2–0.5 nats / d with one token and 1.7–3.5 with 128; oracle_fact − oracle is 0 at d = 1 and grows to 0.19–0.27 nats / d at n = 128.
  • Few tokens: the propagation works. For n ≤ 2 the gap is ≤ 0.08 nats / d at every d (D1: 0.02–0.07), and at n = 1 the model matches oracle_fact at d = 2 and beats it at d = 4, 8 (it keeps the hypotheses joint, which no per-dimension head can).
  • The gap grows with n, at every d. D1, Δ / d at n = 8 / 32 / 128: d = 1 0.11 / 0.17 / 0.20, d = 2 0.17 / 0.28 / 0.39, d = 4 0.18 / 0.34 / 0.61, d = 8 0.14 / 0.29 / 0.49. The oracle sharpens fast with n (§ 2); the model follows more slowly.
  • Most of the gap is the multi-hypothesis case. With one hypothesis (M = 1, pure interpolation) D1's gap stays at or below 0.10 nats / d for d ≤ 2 and reaches 0.12–0.24 for d = 4, 8 at n = 128. With M ≥ 2 it is several times larger, and from n ≈ 4–8 on the model is worse than oracle_fact: it does not track which component belongs to which hypothesis across many tokens as sharply as the labelled oracle. Part of this is the oracle's unfair advantage (it is told the labels); how large that part is, this experiment cannot say (an unlabelled reference is open).
  • The GMM head does carry joint structure. The model's own product of marginals is 0.17–0.30 nats / d worse than its joint at n = 128 (§ 4, last column); the d = 2 example (§ 7b) shows two joint modes and no "ghost" modes at the mixed combinations, but each mode too wide, and at a query where the modes are close they merge.
  • Training budget matters. Doubling the steps and loosening the clip halved the d = 1, 2 gaps at n = 128 (0.38 → 0.20, 0.70 → 0.39) and validation NLLs were still falling over the last 30 % of both runs, for every d (§ 6; the learning rate decays there too). So part of the "gap grows with n" is undertraining; the run does not show where it would saturate.

Reading for the idea. As a mechanism, GMM tokens with self- and cross-attention do propagate a displacement belief, including its joint multimodality, and the cost is linear in d. At this budget the propagated GMM is much less sharp than the Bayes predictive once there are more than a handful of tokens, and most of the loss is in keeping the hypotheses apart, which is exactly what the later B-lookup needs. Before investing further, the cheap next steps would be: (1) a longer training run (validation was still falling); (2) an unlabelled reference for M ≥ 2 (e.g. sampling the per-token assignments), to separate the learnable gap from the cost of not knowing the labels; (3) hypothesis identity as an explicit slot (e.g. components sorted or keyed by weight) to see whether the correspondence, not the interpolation, is the bottleneck.
